INTRODUCTION

Augustine left Carthage with nostalgia. He was looking for Ariadne's thread to get out of his labyrinth—the labyrinth of the heart and intelligence. God weaved and unweaved, and his divine Providence was suggesting the paths of that royal road that led to the eternal city {Confess. V 8,14-15). Rome was a dream and now it could be a reality. Agustín deliberately stole from his mother—the mother of tears—and set sail. «The wind blew, filled our sails and the beach disappeared from our sight, where my mother, the next morning, went mad with pain, filling your ears with complaints and moans, which did not pay attention to them, rather you let me run after my passions to put an end to my concupiscences and punish her with the just blow of pain for her carnal desire» (ibid.). Aguslín had already ringed Rome. Rome, full of lights, gazed in astonishment at that star that longed to shine in its crown. Agustín walked through its streets with his forehead crestfallen, his bearing graceful and light and, yet, amazed. The Rome of the Caesars now sheltered a fugitive. The motives that guided him to the big city are known. Augustine himself expresses them in these terms: "Because my determination to go to Rome was not to win more or achieve greater glory, as the friends who advised me to do so promised me—although these things also weighed on my mind at that time—but the greatest and almost sole cause was having heard that the young people of Rome were calmer in classes thanks to the rigorous discipline to which they were subject, and according to which it was not permissible for them to enter the classrooms of the teachers often and turbulently. They were not theirs, nor even entering them without their permission..." (ibid.). But, we know, Augustine was fleeing his homeland harassed by his conscience; He fled because flight, as he would say, is the path that the heart finds in the midst of its anguish (ibid., IV 7-12). The reality was very different from what the dreamer imagined. In Rome there was discipline, but nobility was lacking (ibid., V 12,22). This fact was the leitmotif of his lamentation over the City, as Christ and Jeremiah did on other days about the
GENERAL INTRODUCTION
INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF I, A «CITY OF GOD»

pleasant Jerusalem. Rome would fall, because its nobility—that of the Romans—was simply culture. It was not hidden from Augustine that the nobility of the citizens keeps the republic standing, because civitas in civíbus est, non in parietibus (De urbis excidio 6,6). And that being noble is not being gregarious or average. In the nobility there is a very deep reality. It is the victory of societies. Frankness, union, nobility, chivalry, everything, except simulation. In Rome people lived by tradition, but, in theory, the experience of that tradition was banished. Discipline, yes; salary, no. And the students—r-the revolutionaries of the capitals—knew how to take advantage of the revolts. Augustine refused to believe, but had to succumb to the obviousness of the facts (Confess. V 12,22). His Rome—the Rome of his dreams—had collapsed. Rome was the home of all sects. The Manichaeans hid there (ibid., V 10,19), there a thousand and a thousand philosophies were professed, including academic ones (ibid.). It was a hive and a swarm. Agustín, with accurate vision, realized the significance of these events. This city will provide you with abundant subject matter for this other one. Living experience always springs up at the right moment.

The theory of two loves as motives of human powers is already a well-worn theme in the writings of the Doctor of Grace \ And this is precisely the central theme of the work. Without wanting to be more Augustinian than Augustine, we will say that the sacking and desolation of Rome was nothing more than a historical circumstance that providentially found an interpreter. I believe well founded that this situation was a stratagem of Providence to give the world a work of this style. Saint Augustine, always fond of seeking Providence as the ruler of everything, even "the little wing of the bird and the little flower of the grass" (De civ. Dei V 11), could not consider his magnum et arduum opus (ibid., I pref.) as the work of chance, but as a providential creation. And so it was. Saint Augustine places his work at the feet of Providence, and all of it is just that, a canticle to Providence.
THE OCCASION, THE PROVIDENCE

The influence, or rather the thrust of Alaric's sacking of Rome as an occasion, as a cause of Augustine's masterpiece, the City of God, has been exaggerated, perhaps more than is fair. It is and has been a topic for all historians and expositors.' It is true that chapter 43 of Book II of the Retractions has given rise to this, where Augustine explains the time of the composition of his work. But the general doctrine of the Hipponense has been forgotten. It is an ambitious pretension to want to look for a motive foreign to Agustín's mind. A question immediately arises: Without the sacking of Rome, would the City of God have been written? We do not believe Papini's abrupt statement to be correct: "Perhaps," he says, "those books would never have been written without the malevolent exploits of Alaric." I would dare to say that this work, if not systematically, then schematically, was written before it was written. Perhaps the first ten books, the apology of religion, to which we will refer later, would not have seen the public light if that providential event had not occurred. The opinion is very widespread. Upon opening this work by the Hiponense the reader finds himself with a considerable number of citations, names and dates. It is curious to note Augustine's extensive understanding, especially of the mythologies and mysteries of pagan religions. Where did the Madaura schoolboy surprise these images? Virgil's Aeneid was well known and widely read. Virgil, for him, was the charming poet, the one who attracted his curiosity in those tender years of his youth, when all his desire was "to love and be loved" (Confess. 112,2; III 1,1). Virgil was that poet who in the midst of mythological fables made him cry in his youth, and in his childhood delighted him with a delight very similar to the true one (ibid., I 13,21-22). Virgil was the poet whose verses children learned from their childhood (De civ. The Antiquities of Varro, with its mythical or fabulous theology, its civil theology, and its natural theology, was an encyclopedia of mythology. As a preamble to this study, it is necessary to advance the Augustinian concept of history. Synthesizing and collecting the invaluable studies prepared on this point, we will reduce ourselves to presenting Arnari's conclusions on the object of history, in accordance with the Augustinian doctrine: «The determination of the historical object—he says—includes a triple order of facts. The first includes events in the generic sense of res gestae. In it we find the locutions spatia ternporum, volumina temporum, contextus ordo saeculorum, series saeculorum, ordo temporum, which indicate the temporal order and the orderly development of events in it. The second order determines the nature of these facts, referring them to men and the action of God in time: gesta divina et humano. The third order specifies the scope of human events, placing the human race as a collectivity as the proper object of history. The object of history is formed by exclusively human knowledge, by scientia. But a higher historical knowledge, sapientia, will manifest another order of facts as the object of history: such is that of the internal struggle of the individual, which is transported to the history of angels and the human race. Let us advance here a term that, without prejudging this problem, will lead us to the end. The term used by us is "hermeneutics of history." Hermeneutics—so overused today, precisely because man is the center of things—implies an interpretation, a subjective element, in which the objection against it will lie. Saint Augustine explains the word épunvda. It means interpretation (De civ. Dei VII 14). The facts themselves do not contain any concrete and determined meaning. The facts are such in relation to this or the other who considers them. Isolated, independently of a subject that gives them a meaning, better yet, an interpretation, they are nothing more than mere effects produced by a cause, which will sometimes be rational, man; sometimes natural, we would say irrational, animals or elements. It will be objected that in this sense we convert history into pure subjectivism, into factual, but ideal, awareness of realities. The objection would be worthy of appreciation if our hermeneutics were simply reduced to this. There are still other elements that integrate and outline it, avoiding this difficulty. It turns out that the man who interprets these facts must do so, undoubtedly, with personal criteria; but at the same time there are other stable, fixed and general criteria for all events. These will be the criteria or forms of hermeneutics. Thus, there is neither philosophy nor theology of history; There is a hermeneutics of history, a philosophical or theological interpretation of history.

Christ, in the Augustinian conception of humanity, is everything. He is the new Adam who gives life to the human race, He is the Redeemer who freed us from our fall, He is the only and true Mediator. In Adam all humanity fell, and from then on, from the dawn of our existence, from the first glimpses of paradise, the life of man was a sigh, a longing, a longing for redemption and, therefore, for a Redeemer. Christ was seen from those distances as the future Dominator, the one who would free humanity, broken and torn, from the deep abyss in which it lay. History thus turned towards Christ. And Christ, by accepting his incarnation, accepted the most transcendental of duties: giving a new being to things, to men and to humanity. It would seem that he accepted being the Creator of the new man. There is an expression in the City of God that summarizes this thought of expectation and turning towards Christ. Agustín thought like this: In my being there was a fight, a fight to the death, between two beings who longed to surprise me. Why then can't I deduce that this is history? From this moment Augustine began to be original. The story began under this vision of duality of loves. Augustine transferred the drama of his life to the events of history. In this way, man became involved in the vital current of historical events and provided a new title to hermeneutics. With this great conception all struggles, all wars, would be explained, because all of them would be just that, a fight between two loves: selfishness and charity. Augustine found this contradiction of desires in the deepest depths of his soul. "There are two wills in the soul, because, one of them not being complete, the other part has what this one lacks... In this way, the two wills of mine, the old and the new, the carnal and the spiritual, fought among themselves and, discording, destroyed my soul" (Confess. VIII 5,10). But, above all, a passage from De Genesi ad lüteram shows us all the characteristics of these two loves in which the world abounds. It says like this: «These two loves, one holy and the other unclean; one social, and the other individual; one who looks to the common good for the heavenly society, and the other who seeks his own usefulness in the common good, due to his arrogant desire to command; the one, obedient to God; the other, his emulator; one calm, the other turbulent; one peaceful and the other seditious; one preferring the truth to the praises of those who err, and the other eager for praise; one friendly, the other envious, one wanting for his neighbor what he wants for himself, and the other eager to subject his neighbor to himself; one, ruling his neighbor for his benefit, and the other for his own. These two loves preceded in the angels, one in the good and the other in the bad, and distinguished the two cities, founded on the human race under the admirable and ineffable providence of God, who administers and orders everything created" (De Gen. ad litt. XI 15,20). Here in a few words is the specific character of the two loves. This is one of the greatest discoveries in history: the specification of being by love. Each one is what he loves (Serm. 121,1). If the operation follows the being, the being follows the love and in love it is completed. Precisely in this lies the genius of the conception. All historical works are products of love, holy, social love, or perverse, private, selfish love. Starting from this assumption, it is easy to explain everything. The civil wars, an example in that of Sulla and Marius, were and are the work of the passion for dominion, of praise, of self-love (De civ. Dei II 23,1-2; 14,1-2).

Self-love, one's own honor and one's own glory were the reason why Regulus returned, after haranguing Carthage in the Senate, to his enemies (ibid., I 15,1-2); that Lucretia killed herself for having been raped (ibid., I 19-1-3); that Cato took his own life for not supporting Caesar's victory (ibid., I 23-24); and this same passion was the cause of death being inflicted on Romulus's brother (ibid., III 6). With this new point of view the hermeneutics of history is completed in what it has of human history, of human freedom. It is not only Providence that is the actor in this historical drama; Christ alone is not the exclusive end of this epic of humanity. He also takes part in it, and as the protagonist to a certain extent, man, this concrete man, with his eternal destiny and his radical Christocentrism. This man who, while traveling on this pilgrimage, carries the sign of transcendence, that of the Augustinian uti, which means journey; not that of frui, which indicates rest, joy, enjoyment. This man gives history a direction according to his love; That is why love is the pivot of history, because man is the active part of it, because, as the being of man is concretized by what he loves, the being of history under Providence and in the direction of Christ is centralized by the love of the one who weaves this story. Thus, the exact vision of history for Saint Augustine is a hermeneutics of historical facts, founded on certain criteria of interpretation, which he uses in the City of God and which are personal and constant, and these are the three pointed out: Providence, Christ and the two loves, which are identified with man.

The literary style, sweet and tasty, rich in rhythm and melody and full of periods, that can be seen in the City of God, makes the translator's job difficult. In reality, in San Agustín two styles are perfectly distinguished, although not completely different, but in their structure. One is the rhetorical style, polished and with a Ciceronian taste, in which the phrase is lengthened and prolonged indefinitely in symmetrical and asymmetrical periods, with rhythm and poetry, but which for translation is often difficult, because sometimes the phrases cannot be reduced, the translator seeing the need to add something from his own harvest, so that, when dividing the phrase, it does not remain meaningless. The reader will be able to appreciate it, and will know how to excuse it, for the sake of intelligibility. There is another genre of style, which is spontaneous, that of the heart, we would say. The heart, when it speaks, has no words to express itself; What he longs for is enough for him. Thus it flashes in pulsating sparks of life, in short, polished phrases, yes, but always intelligible and always profound, just as the ideas of the heart are profound, because the heart also has them. And Agusttín is a genius in this genre. The Confessions, the Letters, the Sermons, all the intimate and circumstantial works are of this genre, because, when Augustine spoke, he spoke from the heart and deprived the tongue of his words. The periods here are short and easy to understand, because another heart can easily understand the reasons of the heart, but not the reasons of the intelligence, which is what happens in the City of God and in the Dialogues of Casiciaco. Precisely all the difficulty for an accessible translation of this great work lies in this, that the City of God is a work of long periods, of subordinate sentences, which acquire a disproportionate length and make the work extremely difficult. Faced with this difficulty, we have sought and attempted mainly two things: intelligibility and literality, but not excessive. The first, because in many passages the reader wants to resolve some doubts, and, if intelligibility is lacking, they remain as obscure as before. The second, because using an openly free sense is undoing the text of its true and typical content. We believe that the translation should be as faithful as possible, without going overboard on one side or the other, neither by meticulous literalness nor by undue freedom. We have tried to

WHAT WAS CRUDITY IN THE DESTRUCTION OF ROME HAPPENED ACCORDING TO THE USAGE OF WARS, AND WHAT WAS CLEMENCY WAS COMING FROM THE POWER OF THE NAME OF CHRIST. Therefore, everything that took place in the last sack of Rome—ruin, blood, theft, fire, and affliction—is the work of the warlike style. However, what was done in a new style, such as choosing and determining the very spacious basilicas that were to be filled by the public blessed with forgiveness, where no one was killed and no one was robbed, where many were taken by pious enemies to escape and from where no one was taken to find themselves in the hands of cruel enemies, this must be attributed to the name of Christ and to Christian times. He who does not see this is blind; He who sees it and does not praise it is ungrateful; and he who resists him who praises him is an idiot. Who who considers himself sane would dare to attribute this to the ferocity of the barbarians? The one who had predicted so long before by his prophet: I will visit their wickedness with a rod and their sins with stripes, but I will not spread my mercy on them, that same one was the one who made their truculent and most brave minds tremble, the one who stopped them and the one who miraculously tempered them.

We would spend forever reviewing the disasters caused in the Second Punic War by these two peoples, who fought so much and in so many places with each other, to such an extent that, according to the confession of those who intended not so much to make a history of the Roman wars as to praise their empire, the victor seemed more defeated. When Hannibal's uprising in Spain, having passed the Pyrenees mountains, crossed France and broken the Alps, increased his forces with so much detour, destroying and subduing everything and bursting into Italy like a flood torrent, how many and how bloody wars were fought and how rude combats! How many cities surrendered to the enemy and how many were taken and plundered by force! How hard battles and how glorious so many times for Hannibal, with destruction for the Romans! And what will I say about the defeat, marvelous in its horribleness, of Cannae, where Hannibal, being so cruel, already dripping the blood of his most bitter enemies, is said to have ordered them to be forgiven? From there he sent three gold rings to Carthage to signify that such was the case.

But, among all the evils of the Second Punic War, none was more unfortunate or more worthy of tears than the destruction of the Saguntines. This city of Spain, so addicted to the Roman people, was destroyed to preserve its loyalty. Hannibal, taking his footing from here, broken his alliance with the Romans, looked for an opportunity to provoke them to war. It barbarously surrounded Sagunto. Who will tolerate that, by choosing the days, some new fates arise for their actions? SIMILARITY AND CONCORD BETWEEN FABULOUS AND CIVIL THEOLOGY

1. Fabulous, theatrical, scenic theology, heavy with indignities and clumsiness, is reduced to civil theology. And this, which is judged, and rightly so, worthy of censure and contempt, is part of the other that is considered worthy of worship and practice. When I say a part, I certainly do not mean a part that is incongruous and foreign to the total body, that is united and dependent on it, but as if out of place, but rather a part that maintains absolute harmony with it and the most proportionate union, as a member of the body. What else do the statues, figures, ages, sexes and ornaments of the gods highlight? Do poets have a bearded Jupiter and a beardless Merc, and don't the pontiffs have them? Did the mime representations, and not also the priests, cause enormous embarrassment to Priapus? Is it one who stands in sacred places for worship, and another who goes out to the tables for ridicule? Don't the actors embody the person of the old Saturn or the pubescent Apollo just as the statues in the temples represent him? Why are Forculus, who presides over the doors, and Limentinus, who presides over the lymens, male gods, and among them Cardea, who guards the openings, is female? Are these details not found in the books of divine things, which the gravity of the poets creates?

1. Animals, they say, are divided into three classes: into gods, men, and demons. The gods occupy the highest place; men, the most humble, and demons, the middle; because the mansion of the gods is heaven; that of men, the earth, and that of demons, the air. As the dignity of places is diverse, so is that of natures. That is why the gods are better than men and demons, and men are inferior to the gods and demons. According to the order of elements, thus the difference in merits. The demons, being in the middle, must be postponed to the gods, to whom they are inferior in place, and put themselves before men, over whom they dwell. They have in common with the gods the immortality of bodies, and with men the passions of the minds [49]. Therefore, it is no wonder, they say, that they delight in the obscenities of games and the fictions of poets, since they are the prey of human affections, from which the gods are far removed and are absolutely foreign to them. From this we conclude that Plato, when he censors and prohibits poetic fictions, deprives the voluptuousness of scenic games, not to the gods, who are all good and excellent, but to the demons.

When the aforementioned Platonist speaks of the customs of demons, he says that they are agitated by the same disturbances of mind as men, with the same irritated insults, with the same gifts and gifts appeased. He also says that they enjoy the same honors, that they delight in various religious rites, and that they get angry if anything is neglected in them. He adds, among other things, that the divinations of the augurs, the haruspices, the poets and dreams belong to them, and that the miracles of the magicians also come from them. Give a brief definition of them in these terms: Demons are, in general, animals; in spirit, passive; enmente, rational; in body, aerial, and in time, eternal. Of these five things, the first three are common to them and to us; the fourth is their own, and the fifth they have in common with the gods. But note that of the first three, common with us, they also have two in common with the gods. The gods are animals, according to Apuleius, who, by distributing each of their elements, placed us among the terrestrial animals, with the others that live and feel on the earth; among the aquatiles, the fishes and other natals; among the aerial ones, the demons, and among the ethereal ones, the gods. 1. It is noteworthy that this Egyptian, when he laments that the time will come in which that cult will be abolished in Egypt, a cult that he confesses was instituted by those who err a lot, by unbelievers and by those separated from the cult of divine religion, says among other things: "Then this land, the most holy habitations of works and temples, will be covered with tombs and the dead." As if men had not died, let us not succumb to that cult, or as if the dead could be given another place than the earth. It is true that the more times and days pass, the more and more there will be tombs, because there will be more and more dead. But it seems that his lament is directed to the fact that the memories of our martyrs were to succeed their temples and works. This means that those who read this, with a spirit adverse to us and perverse, will judge that the pagans worshiped the gods in the temples and we pay tribute to the dead in the tombs. Such is the blindness of godless men that they stumble, so to speak, against the mountains. They do not want to see the things that hurt their eyes and they do not notice that in all pagan writings there are hardly any gods who have not longed for men and, once dead, have paid them divine honors. Porphyry promises, as if hesitant and in a somewhat shameful speech, a kind of purification of the soul by means of theurgy. But he denies that this art brings anyone the return to God. I say this so that you can see that he fluctuates in his alternative feeling between the vice of sacrilegious curiosity and the profession of philosophy. Sometimes he warns that they beware of this art, as fallacious, as dangerous in practice and prohibited by the laws [ 29 ], and other times, as if yielding to his panegyrists, he says that it is useful to purify a part of the soul, not the intellectual, which perceives the truth of intelligible things, which have no resemblance to bodies, but the spiritual, which captures the images of corporeal things [ 30 ]. This says that it is made suitable and suitable for the susceptibility of spirits and angels and for seeing the gods, through certain theurgical consecrations, which they call teletas [ 31 ]. He confesses that these theurgical consecrations do not serve to purify the intellectual soul, making it suitable to see God and to contemplate the things that truly are. The spiritual part, according to him, is purified by the theurgist, but so barely that immortality and eternity are not achieved through this purification. He discerns angels from demons, saying that aerial places are the abode of demons, and ethereal, empyrean, places of angels. And he advises gaining the friendship of a demon so that, led by him, each one can rise even a little from the earth after death and say that there is another way to reach the sovereign company of the angels. He states, on the other hand, with a somewhat express confession, that the company of demons must be avoided. He says this where he writes that the soul after death, when paying its penalties, has a horror of the worship of demons, by which it was deceived. And he cannot deny that theurgy, praised by him as the conciliator of the angels and the gods, works jointly with such powers that either envy the purification of the soul or serve the arts of the envious. 1. Porphyry worked with more sanity when writing to the Egyptian Anebonte [ 34 ], where, as a consultant and researcher, he not only discovered sacrilegious arts, but also destroyed them. In it he rebukes all demons, because he says that they are so imprudent that they drag a humid vapor behind them and that, therefore, they do not dwell in the ether, but in the air under the moon, and in the lunar circle itself. However, he does not dare to attribute all the fallacies, malice and ineptitudes that rightly worry him to the demons. He calls, on behalf of others, some good demons, although he confesses that they are all generally reckless. He is surprised that the gods not only flatter themselves with their victims, but also constrain and force themselves to do what men want. Furthermore, if by the body and by incorporeality the gods are distinguished from the demons, how can it be maintained that the sun and the moon and the various stars visible in the sky, which there is no doubt are bodies, are gods? And if they are gods, how do they say that some are beneficial and others evil? And how do the incorporeals come together when they are corporeal? He also asks, as if in doubt, if diviners and miracle workers have more powerful souls or if some spirits come from outside that give them this power. He believes that they come from outside, because magicians use stones

He made the world, and they cannot deny that the world is visible. Whatever is wonderful in the world is undoubtedly less than the world, that is, heaven and earth and everything in them, which are certainly works of God. As he who did it, so the way he did it is hidden and incomprehensible to man. It is true that the miracles of visible nature become popular, because we are seeing them continually; but, if we consider them wisely, they are superior to the rarest and most unusual. A greater miracle is man than the miracle wrought by man [37]. For this reason, God, who made heaven and earth visible, did not deign to make a thousand visible things in heaven and earth to excite the soul, devoted to visible things, to worship Him, invisible. Where and when he does so, depends on his immutable counsel, in whose disposition the future times are held and realized [38]. He moves temporal things and is not temporally moved. He does not know what he must do in any other way than what he has done, and he does not hear those who call upon him in any other way than he sees those who call on him [39]. When his angels listen, He listens in them as in his true temple, not the work of a human craftsman, as in his holy men. This entire narrative has one goal: the perfection of the number six, which is the same day repeated six times, thus completing creation in six days. And this is not because God needed time, as if he could not create all things simultaneously; He, who was to later form the times with congruent movements, but because the number six means the perfection of the works [103].
